title: Nanak at Baghdad
hookLine: Nanak and Mardana at Baghdad, where he speaks of worlds beyond worlds (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)

lines: BABA, AND MARDANA WITH HIS REBAB.
cards: Two travelers have stopped at a great city. One is Baba Nanak. The other carries a rebab, a stringed instrument, and his name is Mardana.
The city is Baghdad, and the var puts their camp outside it, beyond the walls. Bhai Gurdas sets the scene in a single line: here is Baba, and here is Mardana, the rebab player.
Then something happens that makes everything go quiet. Today: karah prashad.

teach.h: A CALL, AND THE CITY FALLS SILENT.
teach.b: Bhai Gurdas says Nanak gave a call, and the world around fell silent, as if in a trance. A holy man of the city, a pir, came to see who this faqir was.

teach.h: SKIES BEYOND SKIES, WORLDS BELOW WORLDS.
teach.b: And in the talk that followed, Nanak spoke of what lies beyond the edges of the known world: skies beyond skies, and worlds below worlds, past anyone's counting. The pir asked to be shown.

In Bhai Gurdas's telling, Nanak took the pir's son with him, and in the blink of an eye showed him those worlds, and they came back carrying a bowl of karah prashad, the sweet offering, from a world below.
You can hold that last part however your tradition holds it. Some readers take it as it's told. Others hear it as a picture.
Either way, the story is about size.
If you learned the Japji in year one, you've heard this in the Guru's own words.

teach.h: STILL, THE FRIEND AT YOUR SIDE.
teach.b: In the twenty-second pauri, Guru Nanak says there are nether worlds below nether worlds, and skies above skies. People have tried to find the limit, and they can't.
If it could be written down, someone would write it, but the writing would run out first. The pir's world had edges.
Nanak's answer took the edges away, not to make anyone feel small, but to make God large: whatever you've counted, the Creator is beyond it.
And notice who is in the scene's first line: Baba, and Mardana, the rebab player. Even a story about countless worlds starts with a musician sitting beside his friend outside the walls.

how: Sikhs retell Guru Nanak's visit to Baghdad from Bhai Gurdas's first var, and connect his words there to the Japji's teaching that creation has no limit anyone can count.

o: a holy bread baked only for the Gurus' meals
a prayer said over food before a meal
the sweet offering, shared alike with everyone

games.q: inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Bhai Gurdas names Mardana, the rebab player, at his side.
Nanak's words at Baghdad echo the Japji
pauri 22: nether worlds below nether worlds, skies above skies.

games.q: you're the pir of a great city. a traveling faqir is camped outside the walls, and you ask him: how far do the worlds go?
o: just this one, the world we stand on.
as far as the books have counted.
skies beyond skies, worlds below worlds, past counting.
games.why: in Bhai Gurdas's telling, Nanak speaks of worlds beyond worlds, as the Japji does: if it could be written down, the writing would run out first.

practice: If it's dark, look up at the night sky from a door or a window, find the farthest light you can see, and remember that it's not the edge; if it's daytime, close your eyes and picture the sky over your roof at midnight.
Let your breath slow down under all that size; you don't have to understand any of it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, wonder, to the dark.

wordCard.voice: Karah prashad, the sweet offering Nanak and the pir's son brought back from a world below, in Bhai Gurdas's telling of worlds beyond counting.

carryVoice: Your line: worlds beyond worlds. The writing runs out before the wonder does. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauris 35–36 (Nanak and Mardana at Baghdad)
